3-stack Card Trick explanation sought

What I will explain is a card trick for which the outcome has nothing to do with deception.

Begin by turning a full set of playing cards (52 cards) face up and look at the value of the first card, if it is Ace (1) or King (13) put it back anywhere in the deck, if it is any other value (2 - 12) for example 5 put the card on a surface face up and place the next card in the deck on top of it, lay down all cards face up. As you do this you will count from the value of the first cad (5) up to king (13) as such: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 making a pile on the surface of 9 cards. 

Once you've reached 13, turn the pile over (face down) and start again by looking at the topmost card in the remaining deck counting from the value of that card, placing the card in a new pile (face up), count up from the initial value to 13 and turn the new pile over.

Do this until you have 3 piles, keep the remaining cards in the deck.

Now pick two of the three piles that have been counted and laid down and turn the topmost card face up. Add the values of the upturned cards and add 10, for example 5 + 8 + 10 = 23.

Count out 23 cards from the remaining deck of cards that were not placed down into the three piles and remove them from the deck.

When 23 cards have been removed from the remaining deck, the number of cards remaining will be the same amount of cards as the value of the face down card in the third stack that did not have its topmost card revealed.

Is there anyone who can explain why this works?

How to vectorize/matricize Gaussian PDF for more efficient computation?

Context: I was recently implementing the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for Gaussian mixture models, and part of that process involves computing the Gaussian PDF for various points x\_i with various parameters. I implemented it somewhat naively, which was fast enough for what I needed, but I feel like it could be computed faster if it was written in a nice, clean matrix form. However, I don't know how you'd approach getting it in the form you'd need.

&#x200B;

The Gaussian PDF I need is in the form:

p\_k (x\_i | 𝜇\_k, 𝛴\_k)   =   exp(-1/2  (x\_i - 𝜇\_k)^(T)  𝛴\_k^(-1)  (x\_i - 𝜇\_k))   /   \[ (2𝜋)^(d/2)  |𝛴\_k|^(1/2) \]

Notation:

* x\_i is a d-dimensional vector of input data, where 1 ≤ i ≤ N (N is total number of data points)
* *k* ∈ {1, 2, ..., K} is another parameter over which I have to calculate p(x\_i) for each value of *k*
* 𝜇\_k is d-dimensional set of means for the data
* 𝛴\_k is a dxd covariance matrix for the data

(Sorry if it's hard to read.)

&#x200B;

My main points of confusion:

* The equation as I typed above gives a scalar probability for a single *i* and a single *k*.
* I need to calculate it for all i, k, so in the end I'd want an NxK matrix of values.
* The main portion of the exponential part, (x\_i - 𝜇\_k)^(T)  𝛴\_k^(-1)  (x\_i - 𝜇\_k), effectively takes a 1xd vector, multiplies by a dxd matrix, and then multiplies again by a dx1 vector. I don't know how you'd vectorize this for the k's, let alone the i's. For the i's, if you just threw in the entire Nxd input matrix, you'd end up with some NxN matrix at the end, which is not what we want.

Can anyone help me figure out a more elegant way to write this? Again, what I'd ultimately like to end up with is some NxK matrix that I supposed you'd write as: p(X | 𝜇, 𝛴) where X is an Nxd matrix, 𝜇 is a kxd matrix, and 𝛴 is a kxdxd matrix.
